question: What are the scholarly positions on a woman reciting the Qur'an during her monthly cycle?
asked: Her local ulama taught her that she should not recite the Qur'an during her monthly cycle, yet online she sees fatawa from scholars in other countries stating that women can recite the Qur'an during the menses. She is memorizing the Qur'an, and sometimes her cycle lasts many days, more than a week, so her memorization and review are cut off. What are the positions of the scholars regarding a lady reciting the Qur'an during her monthly cycle?
answer:
Now this issue is one that we have to deal with with multiple factors. I want to begin by stating that, Sister Nadia, you're emailing me saying that your local scholars are saying one thing, and my general philosophy and position is that a Muslim should stick with the scholarly consensus within one's own area. That is the best thing to do. You don't want to rock the boat. It's not healthy to have positions that are completely unknown in your community, as long as they're mainstream views, obviously.

And this position that you have been taught is a valid and correct one. It is one that, in fact, the majority of scholars of the past and present have held, and it is true to say that it is the default position of three of the Sunni schools of law. Therefore, if you wish to follow this position and stick with your community's ulama, then that is great. And this position is the position of many of the Sahaba and Tabi'un.

And that is the following: during the monthly cycle that a lady is in, and also the man in the state of janabah (so it applies to the man in the state of janabah, the woman in the state of janabah, and the woman in the state of the monthly cycle; all of that ruling is the same), the majority position is that it is not allowed to recite the Qur'an during that time frame.

And Imam at-Tirmidhi, the famous scholar of hadith, writes in his book, the Jami', that this position is the position of the majority of the companions of the Prophet ﷺ and the tabi'un, meaning their students. It is the position of Sufyan ath-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Shafi'i, Imam Ahmad, Ishaq. And they all said that the ha'id, the lady in the menses, and the junub, the man in the state of janabah, should not recite the Qur'an unless they recite a portion of it, like a du'a, *rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanah*; so that much is allowed. And they allowed such a lady and the man to do dhikr of Allah. And that's the end quote.

So at-Tirmidhi is stating that the majority position is that it is not allowed, unless they state a portion of the verse for the sake of du'a, for the sake of barakah, but not as an act of worship or as a tilawah of the Qur'an. And he then says, but of course it is allowed to do dhikr: subhanAllah, alhamdulillah, la ilaha illallah, du'as, all of that is allowed. But the recitation of the Qur'an would not be allowed during that state.

Now, what is the main evidence that these ulama and the great scholars of the past have? And remember, this is the position of the majority of the ummah. You have the Hanbali position, you have the Hanafi position, you have the Shafi'i position, and it is also the explicit opinion of a number of companions and their students, the tabi'un. What is the evidence that they use? Well, again, I'll just quote you one or two evidences, then we'll move on to the next position.

The most authentic evidence they use is not quite explicit, and that's where the controversy comes. The most authentic, which is in Sahih Bukhari, is a very authentic hadith; the authenticity nobody can deny. The meaning is where it becomes a little bit gray. Aisha, our mother, narrates that the Prophet ﷺ would lean into my room, my chambers.

Now pause here: what does she mean by this? There was a wall between the masjid and the Prophet's house, which was directly connected to the masjid. If you put your hand outside of the wall, you would enter the house of the Prophet; if you put your hand outside the house, you would enter the masjid. So the same wall: on one side of it was the house, on the other side was the masjid of the Prophet ﷺ, with a small gap between, and there are good diagrams online replicating that house. And so if the Prophet ﷺ wanted to, when he was in the mosque, in the state of i'tikaf for example, he could lean back in and lie down; half of his body would be in the house and half of his body would be in the masjid.

And so Aisha radiyallahu 'anha said that he would lean back into my house while I was in the state of menstruation, and he would recite the Qur'an. He would recite the Qur'an while I was in my menses.

Now, how does one derive the prohibition to recite the Qur'an upon the lady in menses based upon this narration? Some of the great scholars, Ibn Daqiq al-'Id, the famous Shafi'i scholar, say that this narration would not have any benefit to derive from it except if it was well known that the lady who is menstruating is not allowed to recite the Qur'an. And therefore the point of the narration comes that it may be recited in front of her, it may be recited in her presence. Otherwise, he is saying, if it was unknown that ladies don't have to recite the Qur'an, what is the purpose of this narration?

And that's an interesting point here. Why would Aisha radiyallahu 'anha make this point of saying, I was in my menses, he would recite the Qur'an? What is the point of that? So Ibn Daqiq al-'Id says the whole point of this is that it was well known amongst the Sahaba that the women would not recite the Qur'an during their time frame, their monthly cycle. And Aisha's narration came to prove that you may recite the Qur'an in her presence; that the man may even lean on his wife, like the Prophet ﷺ would sometimes lean on and lie down, and his head would be on the lap of Aisha radiyallahu 'anha. That doesn't mean anything. You may do dhikr and recite the Qur'an; you may recite the Qur'an even if the lady cannot. That is the position that the majority of scholars have derived from this narration.

There is also another narration which is explicit, but it is not authentic. So in this chapter, the chapter of women reciting the Qur'an, you have one hadith that is authentic but not quite explicit (you have to derive it), and then you have another hadith that is not authentic but it is explicit. And this is the famous hadith which all of the students of knowledge have studied. It is the hadith of Ibn Umar radiyallahu 'anhu, that the Prophet ﷺ said that the lady in menses and the man or woman in the state of janabah should not recite anything from the Qur'an.

And this hadith is explicit, absolutely. It is reported in the Sunan of Ibn Majah. However, pretty much by unanimous consensus of all the scholars of hadith (and why this is the case is beyond the scope of our brief lecture), basically everybody, Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari himself, Tirmidhi himself, Bayhaqi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nawawi, Ibn Taymiyyah, on and on, the list goes on, up until our time, Shaykh Ibn Baz and Shaykh al-Albani, all of them considered this narration to be weak, because it has a well-known weakness. Everybody knows; even the most basic student of knowledge will know that because of a particular narrator this narration is not authentic. And it is well known that in our shari'ah we do not pass rulings based upon inauthentic narrations.

Therefore, putting these two together, this is their main portion of evidence: that there is a hadith in Bukhari that seems to indicate this, and then there is a hadith in Ibn Majah that is explicit about this point. And as I said, this is the position of the majority of the scholars.

Now, I said there's a dissenting opinion. What is the dissenting opinion? Well, the famous position of the Maliki school of law, that's the fourth and the final school, the Maliki school of law. And also there is a fifth school called the Zahiris, or the literalists. And also you have some of the earlier opinions of Imam al-Shafi'i. Imam Ahmad: it is narrated from him in an opinion that is not the more well-known or accepted one. It is also the position of some of the earlier schools of law that are now defunct, such as the Tabari school of law; Imam al-Tabari, Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, had a school of law. It is also the position of Ibn Taymiyyah, who argued very explicitly for this; Ibn al-Qayyim, his student, very clear in his arguments as well; my own teacher Ibn Uthaymin, rahimahullah; and also the Council of Senior Scholars of Saudi Arabia. And generally they are Hanbali in madhhab, but in this issue they broke away from the mainstream position and they allowed the lady in her menses to recite the Qur'an.

And what is their primary evidence? Their primary evidence, to summarize what Ibn Taymiyyah says in his Fatawa: Ibn Taymiyyah says that during the life of the Prophet ﷺ, during the era of the revelation of the Qur'an, all of the ladies were obviously menstruating, and yet despite that fact there is nothing explicit and authentic in this regard. And therefore, if this was something that would have been forbidden, you would have found multiple hadith; you would have found it to be something well known and narrated. The fact is that we have to derive it from an authentic hadith that is not explicit, and as for the da'if hadith, by unanimous consensus of all the schools of law, we do not base our rulings or our theology on a statement that is not authentically attributed to the Prophet ﷺ.

And Ibn al-Qayyim elaborates on this quite a lot as well. Essentially, I'm paraphrasing, so don't quote me exactly, he's saying that it's really not appropriate for the lady to abandon the Qur'an for so long, and she should also be reciting. And perhaps if she doesn't recite during this long time frame, she will forget what she's memorized, or her routine and habit will be broken. So on what basis are we going to deny her an act of worship that is not explicitly forbidden in any authentic hadith? And of course it's not forbidden in the Qur'an itself. So this is the position of Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim and others: that it is allowed for the lady in the menses to recite the Qur'an, even more so if she is memorizing, or she has a routine and she doesn't want to break the routine, or she is reviewing what she has memorized.

Now, these are the two positions out there. Me personally, in this issue, Allah knows best, I am very, very sympathetic to the default majority position. And you are saying that your own community and society is accustomed to a position, so if you are able to, then stick with that position.

Nonetheless, if you choose to follow what I've just said, that Ibn Taymiyyah and so many great ulama have allowed this based upon their understanding of the evidences, and you feel (this is where I'll make an exception) that staying away from the Qur'an for such a long period of time will impact your memorization, will impact your spirituality, in this case I have no hesitation in saying that you may follow the other opinion. Because it's not a minority position in the sense that it's something extremely unknown. It is one of the major schools of law; it is some of the giants of our religion. So it's not obscure, I should say. I mean, in the grand scale of things it is a minority, but it's not obscure; there's a difference. Obscure is shadh, which means a very small minority, a very small group. And minority and majority, as we know: this would be three schools here, one school there. But the point is that one of the schools of law allows this, along with many of the giants, along with many modern scholars who, when they look at the evidences, feel that perhaps some of the earlier scholars, simply out of the fact that the lady should not pray salah, made an extrapolation that she should not read Qur'an. There's no explicit hadith in this regard.

Now, that having been said, my personal opinion, to be very explicit, is that if you're able to, stick with the majority. They seem to have a good basis, because at the end of the day, why would Aisha radiyallahu 'anha say what she's saying unless it was something that was understood? I'm sympathetic to that. Nonetheless, I'm also sympathetic to Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim when they say this isn't good enough, that the evidence is obscure (ambiguous is a better term, not obscure), and that there are no narrations, despite the fact that half the society or more is female; there are no explicit authentic narrations. And so why prohibit somebody from doing something that would make them closer to Allah?

So again, my position is: obviously, if you are a Maliki, then no problem, you're following your school. If you are one of the other three schools, stick with your schools if you're able to; that's the best thing to do. However, if you genuinely feel it's going to be something that will be detrimental... Because I've memorized the Qur'an, I know what it is. When you're in the mood, when you're doing it every day, and then you stop. I remember, subhanAllah, when I was memorizing the Qur'an, if I went on a journey for a day or two and I stopped my memorization, it would impact me. It would impact the swiftness of my memorization; it would impact my muraja'ah, my reviewing. And obviously you are saying your menstruation is longer than a week, maybe ten days, let's say, so one third of the month. So only twenty days you're memorizing, ten days you're not; your whole routine is messed up.

If that is the case, then if you choose to follow the other position, don't make a big deal. Don't tell your community, don't cause any commotion. In your private life, no problem, you may follow the fatwa of Ibn Taymiyyah and these major scholars, if you feel that it will be better for your iman.

Now, that having been said, before I move on to the next question: this was about the tilawah of the Qur'an, or the memorization of the Qur'an. It was not about touching the mushaf. That is a separate action, and touching the mushaf is a higher category, because even a man or a woman who does not have wudu cannot touch the mushaf. Forget about junub and menstruation; even a man or a woman, it's equal here, doesn't matter: if you don't have wudu, you cannot touch a copy of the mushaf.

And this is the explicit position of all of the Sahaba who have an opinion on this issue; there is no dissenting voice amongst the Sahaba. And it is the position of all of the schools, the four schools of law. And there are over 20 of the earliest scholars of Islam, and we don't even know a single person who went against them in the earliest time of Islam. And it is something that is well known, that this was their position.

It is narrated that Salman al-Farsi radiyallahu 'anhu, the Sahabi of the Prophet ﷺ: a group of people were traveling with him, and he went to relieve himself, and then he came back. And then his students said, O respected Shaykh, O teacher, can you do wudu? We want to ask you the tafsir of a verse. So the students of Salman al-Farsi requested: we want to talk about the tafsir of a verse, so can you please do wudu? Salman al-Farsi, the famous Sahabi, said: Go ahead and ask me; I am not going to touch the Qur'an. When you touch the Qur'an, you need to have wudu. So he explicitly said this.

And there is a hadith, of course, that is authentic in this regard, reported by Abu Dawud and Imam Ahmad and others, that our Prophet ﷺ said that none should touch the Qur'an except if they are pure. And when the Qur'an or Sunnah uses tahir, they mean pure in the technical sense, meaning having done wudu. This is an explicit hadith: none should touch the Qur'an except if they have taharah. And the taharah here clearly means the issue of having wudu when you touch the mushaf.

Therefore, if you wish to memorize and you're in your monthly cycle, in this case you should not physically touch your hand to the mushaf. You have a number of options. Either you can use a computer screen and your mouse, and you are not touching the mushaf if you do that. Or you use an iPad or iPhone and use some type of instrument or rubber pen or something to go over it. Or if you have no other option except a physical copy of the mushaf, in this case you will wear a glove. Just like if I don't have wudu and I wanted to touch the Qur'an, I would put some covering. And that is why in our culture it is very common for the mushaf to have a covering, because you don't need to have wudu to touch the covering. And that's the reason why in our cultures, so many cultures, the Qur'an has a covering: in case you need to pull it down, in case you need to move it from place A to place B, that covering will do the job.

Therefore, bottom line: **in your monthly time frame, if there's a reason to, you may follow the minority position and recite or memorize the Qur'an. However, in that time frame you cannot touch the mushaf.** You must use either a third-party mechanism, let's call it, which is like a computer screen, or you may use an actual copy, but you do not touch it; use a glove or use a pencil to move it. Of course you can see it, no problem, but you cannot use your bare hands to touch the sacred book. And this applies to men and women who don't have wudu, because we respect the Qur'an as the book of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.
